stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Planting cover crops between cash-crop seasons can rebuild depleted soil, but species differ sharply in what they contribute. In a four-year field trial on Iowa farmland, agronomist Renata Okafor compared three candidates: hairy vetch, a legume whose root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen; cereal ______ buckwheat, a broadleaf that flowers within six weeks and crowds out early weeds.
choices: rye; which scavenges nitrate left in the soil, and
rye, which scavenges nitrate left in the soil, and
rye, which scavenges nitrate left in the soil; and
rye: which scavenges nitrate left in the soil; and
explanation: This sentence lists three cover crops, and each one comes with a describing phrase set off by a comma ("hairy vetch, a legume..."). Because the items already contain commas, the list has to use semicolons between items, and the first item already ends with one ("...atmospheric nitrogen;"). So the second item has to follow the same pattern as the first. The comma goes between the crop and its description ("cereal rye, which scavenges..."), and the semicolon goes between this item and the next one ("...in the soil; and buckwheat"). Only choice C puts both marks where they belong.

A.why: You saw that this list needs a semicolon, but you put it in the wrong place. A semicolon after "rye" cuts the crop off from its own description, which leaves "which scavenges nitrate left in the soil" stranded as a fragment. Then the real break between items gets only a comma. Knowing the list uses semicolons isn't enough. You also have to check that the semicolon sits between two items, not inside one.

B.why: This is the trap the question is built around. The comma after "rye" makes a comma before "and" look natural, like an ordinary serial comma. But the first item ends with a semicolon, and its own describing phrase already uses a comma. If you use only commas here, the reader can't tell where one crop ends and its description begins. You decided from the nearby words without checking how the rest of the list is punctuated.

D.why: A colon can't go here. The colon after "candidates" has already introduced the list, and a second colon after "rye" would mark the middle of an item as a new introduction. What comes before a colon has to be a complete sentence that sets up what follows. "Cereal rye" is just one list item, so the colon breaks the item in two.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Materials scientist Ines Varga has spent two decades developing what she calls "forgiving" materials: polymers that seal their own cracks when gently ______ ceramics that flex under loads that would shatter ordinary porcelain, and alloys that spring back to a programmed shape after being bent; the appeal of all three, she argues, is that a damaged part need not be thrown away.
explanation: The colon introduces a list of three materials, and the blank falls between the first and second items. None of the items contains a comma of its own. Each is a noun followed by a "that" clause with no commas inside it, so the list needs only commas, and the separator before "and alloys" is a comma. To match it, the blank needs a comma too. The semicolon later in the sentence isn't part of the list. It joins two complete sentences: the list sentence and "the appeal of all three...is that a damaged part need not be thrown away." The commas around "she argues" belong to that second sentence, not to any list item.

A.why: You looked past the blank for a semicolon and found one, but it doesn't separate list items. It comes after the last item and joins two complete sentences. The commas around "she argues" sit in the second of those sentences. The list items themselves have no internal commas, and the separator before "and alloys" is a comma. A semicolon at the blank would give the list two different separators.

C.why: The colon after "materials" has already introduced the list. A second colon partway through the list would mark the first item as the setup for the rest, when in fact it's just one item in a series. Colons don't separate items in a list.

D.why: With no punctuation, the first two items run together: "when gently warmed ceramics that flex" reads as if "warmed" described "ceramics." The polymers and the ceramics are separate items, so there has to be a separator between them, and it should match the comma used before "and alloys."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The 1782 revision of the Halvorsen coastal atlas added three features that its earlier editions lacked: a grid of latitude lines______ a table of distances between harbors, compiled from more than two hundred ships' logs; and an index that, for the first time, listed each place-name in both Danish and Latin.
explanation: The colon introduces a list of three features. The second item has an internal comma ("harbors, compiled from..."), and the last item opens with "; and." Once any item has internal commas, semicolons have to separate all the items, including the first two. The first item is short and has no comma of its own, but that doesn't change the rule. Check how the rest of the list is punctuated, and you get a semicolon.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. You looked only at the short first item and used a simple series comma. The list already uses semicolons further on because a later item has an internal comma, so every item must be separated the same way.

C.why: A colon has already introduced the list. A second colon here would treat "a grid of latitude lines" as a complete sentence that sets up an explanation, but it's only a phrase in the list.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon, so it would make the distance table read as an explanation of the grid. That breaks the list of three. Nothing later closes it as a pair, either.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Excavations at the hilltop site turned up three kinds of evidence for year-round settlement: storage pits lined with clay; hearths rebuilt so often that their ash lay in forty distinct layers, each______ by the excavators' count, marking a single season of use; and the bones of migratory birds that pass through the region only in winter.
explanation: The blank isn't between two list items. It's inside the second item, at the start of the interrupter "by the excavators' count," which is already closed by the comma after "count." A comma has to open it to match. Cross out the interrupter and you get "each marking a single season of use," a phrase that belongs to the hearth item. The real item boundaries are the semicolons after "clay" and "use."

A.why: You saw a semicolon list and put a semicolon at the blank. The blank falls inside the hearth item, though, not at an item boundary. A semicolon would cut off "each" as if it were a list item and leave the closing comma after "count" without a partner.

B.why: The interrupter already has its closing comma after "count." Leaving out the opening comma leaves that comma unpaired, so the interruption is punctuated at only one end.

D.why: A dash can open an interruption, but then a dash has to close it. Here the interrupter closes with a comma, and punctuation around an interruption must match at both ends.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The orbiting telescope carries three instruments: a camera that records red, green, and near-infrared light______ a spectrograph that splits incoming starlight into thousands of narrow bands; and a small coronagraph, which blocks a star's glare so that faint companions can be seen.
explanation: The commas just before the blank belong to a smaller list inside the first item (red, green, and near-infrared). The separator for the main list shows up later, at "; and a small coronagraph." Because the first item contains commas, the three instruments have to be separated by semicolons. Matching the commas right next to the blank gets the level of the list wrong.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap, in a second-order form. You matched the commas closest to the blank, but they separate colors inside one item, not instruments. The main list uses semicolons, as "; and" shows later.

C.why: With no punctuation, the camera item runs straight into the spectrograph item ("light a spectrograph"), and nothing marks where one instrument ends and the next begins.

D.why: A colon has already introduced the list. A second colon would present the spectrograph as an explanation of the camera's light, not as the next instrument in the series.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Surviving pattern books from the Lyon silk trade record, for each design, three things: the weave structure, often sketched on squared paper; the number of shuttles required______ the name of the merchant who commissioned it. Few of the books note the weaver at all.
explanation: The first item has an internal comma ("structure, often sketched"), so the list is separated by semicolons, and the first separator already is one. The last two items have to be separated the same way, so "; and" goes before the final item. The short second item doesn't change this. The separator is set by the list as a whole.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. "Shuttles required, and the name" reads like an ordinary series comma because the nearby items are short. The list already separates its items with semicolons, though, and the final separator has to match.

B.why: With no punctuation, "the number of shuttles required and the name of the merchant" joins into one item. That leaves only two items, while the text promises "three things."

C.why: A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and "the number of shuttles required" is only a phrase. Inside a list, a colon also wrongly makes the merchant's name sound like an explanation.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: An inventory of the Ferrand print shop, taken in 1791, lists its most valuable holdings: forty copper plates, most of them engraved with maps; a press—its frame built of oak, iron, and brass______ that could print a full folio sheet in a single pull; and three hundred reams of rag paper.
explanation: The dash after "press" opens an interruption, and the blank is where it has to close. Cross out "its frame built of oak, iron, and brass" and you get "a press that could print a full folio sheet in a single pull," which is complete as a list item. A dash that opens an interruption must be closed by a dash. The semicolons around the item mark the list boundaries and don't affect this.

A.why: The commas in "oak, iron, and brass" made a comma look natural. The interruption opened with a dash, though, and you can't open with a dash and close with a comma.

C.why: You saw a semicolon list and put a semicolon here. The blank falls inside the press item, so a semicolon would leave the dash unclosed and turn "that could print..." into a stray fragment.

D.why: With no punctuation, the dash never closes, and "brass that could print" makes it sound as if the brass, not the press, prints the sheets.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The trial, which ran for six seasons at a research station near Ames, Iowa, rotated three crops through each plot—corn______ soybeans, and oats—and found that the rotation, compared with corn grown alone, cut fertilizer needs by nearly a third.
explanation: The list itself is corn, soybeans, and oats. These are three single words with no internal punctuation, already separated by a comma before "and oats." Simple items take commas. The commas elsewhere in the sentence belong to the "which" clause and the "compared with" interrupter, not to any list item, so they don't call for semicolons.

A.why: The sentence is full of commas, so you reached for a semicolon. Those commas belong to the main clause, not to the list items. The crops are simple items, and the comma before "and oats" shows the list already uses commas.

B.why: A colon after "corn" would make soybeans and oats an explanation of corn, not fellow members of the series, and it would break the list in the middle.

C.why: The dash after "plot" opens an interruption that is meant to close after "oats." A dash after "corn" would close it too early and leave "soybeans, and oats—" stranded.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The 2019 survey of former warehouse employees reported three findings: median wages, which had risen by eleven percent; average weekly hours, which had barely changed; and the share of workers______ who said they would return to their old employer if offered the chance.
explanation: The blank is inside the third item, which begins after "; and." "Who said they would return..." tells you which workers are being counted, so it's essential to the meaning and takes no punctuation. Without it, "the share of workers" has no meaning. The first two items use ", which" because those clauses only add information, but this clause narrows down the group being counted.

B.why: This is a second-order trap. You copied the ", which" pattern from the earlier items. Here the clause defines the group being counted, and setting it off with a comma would make it sound as if all workers said they'd return.

C.why: You put a list semicolon at the blank, but the item boundary is the "; and" before "the share." A semicolon here would split one item into a phrase and a fragment.

D.why: A dash would set off the defining clause as an aside, cutting the counted group off from its description. Nothing closes the dash, either.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Divers surveying the reef in 2024 counted four grazers that had returned after the marine heat wave: purple sea urchins; kelp crabs______ red abalone, which had been absent from the site for nine years; and a single school of opaleye, a fish rarely recorded north of the bay.
explanation: The text promises four grazers: urchins, kelp crabs, abalone, and opaleye. The separator after "urchins" is already a semicolon, and the abalone and opaleye items both contain internal commas, so every item must be separated by a semicolon. The blank falls between the second and third items.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. "Kelp crabs" and "red abalone" are both short, so a comma looked natural. The list already uses semicolons, and the later items have internal commas, so a comma here breaks the pattern.

B.why: A colon has already introduced the list. A second colon would make the abalone an explanation of the kelp crabs, not the next grazer.

D.why: "Kelp crabs and red abalone" turns two grazers into one item. With the final "; and," the list then has only three items, while the text says divers counted four.
